utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you comment on items 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This shows how amateurish this study was, and it shows that the census-takers, if there were any such people, they didn't know what to do, they didn't know how to proceed. I assume that this questionnaire was selected in order to be a valid questionnaire. And if you have a look at question 3, it says "members of households who are now living in the free areas of the city of Sarajevo." And the head of the family household should be listed, and here you have five members of the household listed. The fifth member is Dzedovic Meho, Suhrija. Have a look at question 4. "Members of family households who are -- took refuge or, rather, displaced outside of Sarajevo or remained in the territory of the Republic of BiH which is under the control of the aggressor." And then it says, "Dzedovic Meho, Suhrija and then you have other information. So Dzedovic Suhrija was at the same time in Sarajevo - you can see this in question 3 - and at the same time she was a refugee. You can see that in question 4. So she was in two places at the same time, and this is physically impossible. And if I may, I would like to draw your attention to another fact: The questionnaire here discusses the matter of the status of civilians and soldiers or combatants -- civilians and combatants. Mrs. Tabeau regards, this treats this as if it was civilians and soldiers. So I think that this was an amateurish project and that is also because the term "combatant" and "soldier" in Serbian and Bosnian language don't have exactly the same meaning. In armed conflicts a soldier is always a combatant, but a combatant might be a soldier but is not necessarily a soldier, and it is my opinion that the purpose of this questionnaire was to gather combatants regardless of the fact -- regardless of the fact whether they were soldiers or civilians. I think she said that they were soldiers -- Mrs. Tabeau said they were soldiers because if you compare this to a more reliable source of information, and that is the list of those killed in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the number of those killed will be significantly lower than the number for soldiers -- or rather, than the number provided by Mrs. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, there's no interpretation of what is now being said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Oh, we are -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when polls are conducted that control is conducted directly in the field. Have you ever come across information that such control was done in the field during the polling?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there all right now, for my learned friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe we received the answer, namely that the witness has not found the information that this was subjected to the control in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that your answer?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Madam, I would like you to explain to me a paragraph, a passage which I failed to understand. I'm referring to paragraph D called "Main conclusions" in English, and it is on page 5.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I will quote it in English. You said: [In English] "[Previous interpretation continues] ... On the basis of which absolute values on the total population and its structures, the relative calculation was made. All the relative calculations were made on the basis of 100.000 inhabitants, although this is nonsense." And then you said, "this manner was being employed in order to intensify the impression and to present the event as a major and more significant one." [Interpretation] So my question is: When one uses this method, how can one amplify the result?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that does not happen. But one simply gets a different picture, rather than have the mortality 5 per 1.000, it says it's 500 per 1.000. That is the only difference. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You mean not per 1.000 but per 100.000, but the percentage is the same.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same, but it is presented differently, and this is what the difference is, if I may be allowed to explain. When, for instance, you are presented it per municipalities, you have the municipality of Vogosca, which has a population of 24, 25 thousand, and now you say that the mortality rate in Vogosca is, say, 500, which means that per 1.000 -- per 100.000 population, the mortality rate is 500 and there are 24.000 inhabitants in Vogosca. Demographically and statistically it is correct, but it serves no purpose because Vogosca will have 100.000 population at the end of this century or perhaps it won't. So it is better to say that the rate is 5 per 1.000, that is, that one takes 1.000 inhabitants. I'm saying that the manner of presentation did -- was not appropriate because of the number that we have. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But the result is the same, if I understand properly and therefore, it cannot lead to any confusion.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the result is the same. It cannot result in any confusion. I merely thought that this was the manipulation with the manner of presentation. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but this is a value judgment. You are not contesting it as such. You are simply interpreting it no different, that is, basing it on your personal impression. My second question, please: You told us that the samples that were used in the Tabeau et al. report were based on the number of 85.000. And bearing in mind that in every household there are four persons, one arrives at a total figure, at the total population. So my first question is: Does one use -- if we say that every household has four members, is it in contradiction with the rules normally applied, with standards normally applied in your discipline? Or let me explain it further. When this -- when the Medecins sans Frontieres drafted their report, they found that the population was roughly the same as the size of the population indicated in Madam Tabeau's report. So I deduce from that that to start from an assumption that a household has four members does not mean a deviation, that that is correct to use that. Would that be right? What is your impression and what is your opinion about the size of the household?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing against it. I accept it. Mrs. Tabeau's assumption, I accepted it, and that is the figure that I addressed, the total population 340.000. But Mrs. Tabeau in contrast with those other reports has an assumed area which has not been statistically defined. She says "within the front lines," and she mentions 89 neighbourhood, local communities, and she observes a different period of time, that is, the period of time between 1992 and 1994. And she also has the following information: She say that is the UNHCR say that is in all six Sarajevo municipalities in 1998 there were 72.000-something refugees. We are looking at an area which is smaller than all six Sarajevo municipalities and in which an average household was -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your point of view. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to put a few questions to you. May I perhaps give you a small piece of paper just to clarify my question to you. Could you please put that on the ELMO. I'm trying to draw your attention to a situation that did not exist but just a hypothetical one. We have a small funeral parlour, a smaller one than the Bakija, and let's just assume that the data are reliable but the same would be true if the data are not reliable. In a relevant time and in a relevant period of time they buried 2.340 Muslims. If the PDS 1994 tells us that on the totality of the population covered by the PDS in the same relevant time and in the same relevant period 2.340 Muslims were killed, would that justify the conclusion that no Muslim -- where it says "no one" it should say "no Muslim" -- died from natural causes in that relevant time, relevant period?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I fully understand the question, but I do not think that it should follow. Why not? Because the sources of information are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And neither source is good. If we assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let me just stop you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just assume that the sources are good. So we have a funeral parlour and they inspected every and each individual person buried, and the PDS 1994 was perfect. Would this conclusion -- could that be drawn from the data given?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be statistically accurate. The difference here is zero, therefore it means that no one died of natural causes. But that would automatically tell an expert that something was wrong with some source. Because if we look at it from a purely mathematical point of view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Take my example and tell me what is wrong with the sources. It's a perfect registration by the funeral parlour, and it's a perfect - well, whether you call it census or - let's just assume for the sake of argument that it's perfect. Would this be the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't understand what it says here, but I assume that the first is Bakija and the second here is the census of 1994. And now you tell me Bakija buried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying it's Bakija. I just said to you it's a hypothetical. Call it funeral parlour X, not Bakija. It's a smaller one, in fact, than Bakija. Let's just forget about the existence of Bakija. This is a smaller funeral parlour which in this area would bury Muslims. Then again, my question is: Would this be a conclusion that could be drawn from these figures?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are not a demographer, then yes. And if you are, you start wondering, and that is where I must insist, because the calculations show that it is zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have to know -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of what that funeral parlour is called, it buries everybody in the same area as is covered by the census or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a small funeral parlour. There are others. And there are --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covers the whole area that is covered by the census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They bury people from that same area from all parts but not all of them because there are other funeral parlours who do bury the other persons who died.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. So this is the first source which is doubtful. The second one is the population census. So I ask you: Where did you get to 2.340? What was the source of it? Because that is another hypothesis, that you need to have the two overlap, and it's only apparent -- only apparently nobody died from natural causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The assumption is that the registration by the funeral parlour was perfect, they -- well, they photographed every person, uniforms as well, they got full information, they know exactly whether it's a man or a woman, all is perfect, and the same for the PDS. They double-checked three times all the information. Would this then --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But my question is: How many persons in the PDS were killed and buried by this funeral parlour? Is there a duplication? If 2.340 were killed, according to the PDS, then the assumption is that none of them were buried by this small funeral parlour, that they were all buried elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that to you --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that to you. Part of those killed --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm just asking. I'm asking. A demographer must ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll give you an answer. A number, a higher number or smaller number, but a considerable number of those killed were buried by this funeral parlour.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assumption that 1.340 of those 2.340 were buried by this funeral parlour, then the remaining 1.000 - the remaining 1.000 - in all likelihood died of natural causes because we do not know where this 1.000 is buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why one needs more information if you are to say one thing or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But on the basis of what we see here, we cannot draw the conclusion that no one died from natural sources because the population served by the small funeral parlour will have been a smaller one than the total population. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I get your point. Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I say that on the basis of the assumptions we made you cannot conclude that no one died from natural causes because the -- not everyone was buried, not every Muslim was buried by this small funeral parlour.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can conclude is how many probably died but not how many exactly. If I know the assumption, how many Muslims were killed, and then I have another assumption which says those killed Muslims can be buried only here, there's no other place, only this small funeral parlour, that is -- well, that's what I'm saying. That is the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A killed Muslim may not be buried anywhere else. He must be buried by this funeral parlour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is the case we have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the conclusion would be true.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Then one could differentiate between possible natural deaths and how many are violent deaths. And I think the whole confusion is that I didn't explain it. The condition is the source. The one who buries Muslims, there is no other side which might be burying Muslims. Killed, died of natural causes, wherever, he will always be buried by Bakija. There is nobody else or in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Bakija yet. I'm just talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to this. So the condition must be that nobody may be buried by anybody else. Only this is the way in which we can differentiate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... If my small funeral parlour would bury all Muslims that had been killed in the relevant time, relevant period, only then we could conclude that no one, no Muslim, died from natural sources. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the figures are identical, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now may I take you to page 24 of your report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what page it is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the Bakija -- I think it's page -- let me just have a look. It's page 14 --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. 2.1.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like you to concentrate on what you have written under "A," and I would like to ask you a few questions. The first one is: Did Bakija bury all killed Muslims in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau says - and that is the only source I have - because I don't know. I've never heard of Bakija. And she says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question: Where does Ms. Tabeau say that all killed Muslims were buried by Bakija?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she doesn't say all. She says the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's -- let's just -- yes. So --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find that. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we do agree that Ms. Tabeau does not say that they were all killed -- they were all buried by Bakija. Now we have -- let's just assume that the PDS 1994 is correct and Bakija is giving reliable information. That would mean that your conclusion that the probably death by natural causes would be only a logical conclusion if all killed Muslims would have been buried by Bakija. I think that's the exercise we just did on my smaller funeral parlour, isn't it? Therefore, is the conclusion you draw in respect of 3.926 reliable if we have to assume that Bakija did not bury all of the killed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean whether the figure of 3.926 is accurate or whether the conclusion is accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the conclusion is not accurate, I would say the number would not be accurate either unless by any coincidence, according to a different system, you came to the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is accurate if we accept the assumption that this figure is accurate, regardless of whether they buried all the killed or not. The company buried so many Muslims, regardless of whether they were all killed. So I think that the sample is wrong. The principle is all right, but whether the figure is all right, that is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think that with our smaller funeral parlour we just came to the conclusion that it would only be correct to deduct one from the other if all killed Muslims would be buried by my smaller funeral parlour. That was one of the preconditions for drawing these kind of conclusions, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But in that case, this is the number -- the overall number of the killed Muslims. I suppose that there would be more natural deaths, so that if not 2.340 killed Muslims were buried by Bakija but only 1.000, that is, if half of those killed were buried elsewhere and half by Bakija, then the difference shows that the natural mortality is higher than shown here. It is irrelevant whether all the killed Muslims were buried by Bakija or not. It is irrelevant in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just told us on the basis of my smaller funeral parlour that it's of high relevance for the conclusion whether all killed Muslims were buried by Bakija. That is to say, whether the PDS 1994 covers the same population as the Bakija funeral, that would mean that they would have buried all those people who were subject of the PDS 1994; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We said in the beginning if we have the sum total, then we said if one half of those Muslims were not buried by this small funeral parlour, the difference between those who were buried and that other half who were not buried there would be those who died of natural causes. And if we have such identical figures, that holds true only if they were all buried by this small funeral parlour, then we have no natural deaths. Perhaps you don't understand me. What does matter is which share of those buried are the ones who were killed. That is important. Is that share higher if we are talking about a different area, or perhaps a smaller share if we are talking about a different area? So what is important is whether we're dealing with one and the same area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you should calculate the degree to which the Muslims covered by the PDS 1994 were buried by the funeral parlour in order to draw conclusions. Did you do that on page 24? I see that you just took the number of those buried by Bakija without making any adjustment as to what part of the population would be served by the Bakija funeral parlour.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to bear in mind that I took the figures out of the expert opinion and I took the highest possible figure, that is, the possibility that they were all buried there. And in that case, the mortality rate of natural causes is such. Had I taken one-half only, then the natural causes would account for even a larger percentage. But what I said, the assumption is that they were all -- that all Muslims were killed, and then I got smaller natural mortality. Had I taken it that the half of those killed were buried by Bakija and half of them elsewhere, again the figures would be different. Had I taken -- I mean, these are all the assumptions. These are only guesses. And I'm sure of this. If they're all here, then the probability that I will go round is lesser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this calculation is based on the assumption that all killed Muslims were buried by Bakija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason to accept on the basis of the report by Mrs. Tabeau that all killed Muslims were buried by Bakija?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I have a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Before. I think you then said that it was not, it was only a major part.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a major part or majority. I just want to check because I'm not sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So not all of them. It could be 60 per cent, it could be 70 per cent, it could be 80 per cent. And do you agree that that then would have to be taken into consideration if you make the calculation you make under A?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You need to bear in mind that the calculation was done to show that the sources of information were wrong. I was not trying to show what was more fair, what was more just, and that is why I didn't use any other calculating method. Had I assumed that 60 per cent of the Muslims who were buried there, rather than 100 per cent, then I wouldn't get anything in order to change the expert report because this lady says so many were buried there. And I am reducing the probability that the natural causes account for more per cent if I take that this is 100 per cent. I wouldn't get this difference that the natural causes would be 3.126. It would be less had I not taken that not all the Muslims were buried there. And from that point of view the figure here does not give us other variants. What if 20 per cent were buried there? What if 30 per cent were buried there? Because it makes no sense, for the simple reason that it will only exacerbate the differences, and I believe it shows simply that the sources are bad, that the sources on which all the assumptions and statistical conclusions are based, these sources are poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in understanding that if you make calculations which do not consider the data given by the Tabeau report, one of these data being that the majority but not all of the Muslims, were buried by Bakija, that you could make a calculation which ignores part of the data of the Tabeau report in order to demonstrate that the sources of the report are wrong.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have then to address very many assumptions. When it says the majority of Muslims were buried by Bakija, what is the majority? Anything that is above 50 per cent. It is not said the majority of 80 per cent or 90 per cent. Once again I say if I take it the majority is all, I'm not making a major assumption that such can account for more. Had I taken 60 per cent, 70, or whatever, this is making guesses because nowhere does it say what the majority means. Had I taken even the assumption that it was only 50 per cent, then the difference, that is, in favour of natural causes would be much higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we could easily read that on the basis of these data you should not make such calculations because the data is insufficient to do that. Ms. Tabeau didn't do it. That's -- I mean, you are making the calculation. She did not. In a similar way we asked you several times where she makes similar calculations as you do. I didn't find it in the report. But let's not enter into a debate. You have answered my questions thoroughly. And is there any question that would have come up on the basis of the questions by the Chamber? If not, then the concludes your testimony in this court, Ms. Radovanovic. You've been here for a couple of days. It took a long time. You've answered all the questions put both by the Defence and the Prosecution, by the Chamber, put to you. We thank you very much that you've come the long way to The Hague. We apologise that you had to stay longer than expected under sad circumstances in your country. We wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, please escort Ms. Radovanovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely wanted to say that the Defence has completed its case at this stage in our proceedings, with regard to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it -- yes, because I take it that we -- we still have to deal with the exhibits, and that would be part of your case as well. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is understood. We will first adjourn, and then deal with the exhibits, until quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we please start first with the exhibits introduced through the last expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1927, bundle of documents with the first page bearing ERN number 00982900, in B/C/S; D1927A, the aforementioned exhibit with the pages numbered from page 1 through to 105; D1927.1A, English translation of page ERN 00985639; D1927.1B, English translation of page ERN number 00982954; Exhibit D1927.1C, English translation of page ERN number 00982953; Exhibit D1928, bundle of documents, the first document bearing number 00986277, survey of so far killed and wounded civilians in sniping activities in the town of Sarajevo from 06/09/1992 to 10/08/1994; D1928A, the aforementioned exhibit with numbered pages starting from 1 through to page 132; P3774, forced migration and mortality; .1, B/C/S translation; P3775, demographic assessment techniques in complex humanitarian emergencies; .1, B/C/S translation; P3776, political killings in Kosova/Kosovo March to June 1999; .1, B/C/S translation; P3780, report of a household survey in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina April 1993; .1, B/C/S translation; P3780A, questionnaire Sarajevo; .1, B/C/S translation; P3781, brief report, premature mortality in former Yugoslavia; .1, B/C/S translation; P3782, two-page document, first page bearing ERN number 00986275 and 00986276, both in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not an objection, just a query. In respect to the first two -- or could we call it the first four exhibits, that is, 1927, 1927A, and 1928, and 1928A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two bundles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The two -- what is now four bundles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now four bundles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are we to consider them as completely in evidence or are we entitled to refer only to the pages that were discussed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the documents have been tendered by the Defence. What was your attitude?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is that documents 1927, 1927A, 1928, and 1928A are integral parts of the document 1927. Except that these documents have translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you expect the Chamber to do with those parts not translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence expects that the Chamber will decide that the untranslated parts, that is, in these translations we showed that the parts which are not translated are also integral parts of that same report, which is a document 1927; and likewise, in the document 1928. We, for technical reasons, we simply were unable to translate all these documents, but the document 1928 is -- the expert addressed it in her expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will give you a decision on that, Mr. Stamp, specifically to what extent these documents are integral parts of the evidence. Are there any other objections? If not, then the other documents are admitted into evidence. So not yet 1927 and 1927A as a consequence and the same for 1928 and 1928A. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the registrar has suggested that we are suggesting through General Radinovic we would like to produce documents following the bar table and under numbers -- so statements of experts which are D1917, D1918, D1919, D1920, D1921, D1922, D1923, D1924, and D1925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I -- perhaps I should have -- say whose finding it was alongside every number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the registrar will lead us through that, but I would ask her to limit herself to the expert reports and not yet to the documents to be tendered from the bar table because I do understand that, although we have not thoroughly studied it, that the summary explanation of the Prosecution also deals with documents tendered in this way by the Defence. I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I would -- for example, I see on page 14 of your explanation, Mr. Ierace, that exhibits tendered from the bar table no objections. So I'd rather deal with all the Radinovic documents at the same time rather than -- we should have an opportunity to hear and perhaps first read what the Prosecution has told us in this respect. So therefore, I would first like to concentrate on the expert reports. Madam Registrar, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1917, expert report Janko Vilicic; D1918, expert report Kosta Cavoski; D1919, expert report Slavenko Terzic; D1920, expert report Jelena Guskova; D1921, expert report Dusan Dunjic; D1922, expert report Svetlana Radovanovic; D1923, expert report Blagoje Kuljic; D1924, expert report Milan Kunjadic; D1925, expert report Radovan Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These expert reports and the admissibility of these expert reports has been largely discussed. As far as my recollection goes, there is a last request not to admit finally the Radinovic report. I think we should first study that thoroughly and hear what the Defence has to say on it and then give a final decision. The main reason, I think, why these expert reports are mentioned at this very moment is for the technical reason that they were not, as all the expert reports from the Prosecution were, were formally tendered into evidence. So the decisions in respect of these reports stands as they are, and we still have to give a decision on a new request where the Radinovic report was admitted into evidence to exclude parts or the whole of that report. Then I would like to take the parties back to, I would say, not ancient times but at least in the past. The parties have been provided with lists of documents of exhibits still outstanding, if I am well informed. So let me first go through that list. We first have D1815, which is a pseudonym sheet in relation to Witness DP30, which is tendered to be admitted under seal. No objection. It's then admitted under seal. Then we have P3769, also introduced through Witness DP30, which is photo of sniper rifles. I do not hear any objection, so therefore that is also admitted into evidence. Then one of the outstanding issues was in relation to Prosecution document 3766, 3766.1, and P3766A and P3766A.1 under seal, introduced through Witness DP30. That is a transcript of an interview of Witness DP30 with OTP representatives. On the 10th of December the Trial Chamber has expressed that it would consider admission of the transcript if certain conditions were met. As far as the Trial Chamber is aware, the documents have not been received by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're now in a position to tender the transcript of the interview in the format that the Trial Chamber required. Pardon me, Mr. President. I would therefore seek to tender P3766B and P3766B.1. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think -- well, Mr. President, if you require copies of the cassette tape recorded interview, we have those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The audiotape was one of the conditions. So I think the Chamber would consider admission of the transcript if it would receive the audiotape of the interview, the transcripts in English and B/C/S as seen in court and annotated by the witness, the transcripts of the original words spoken, sometimes called a mixed transcript, and an official translation of the mixed transcript. I think that the Defence should have an opportunity first to look at it and then it would be unfair to ask you to express yourself on this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A decision on 3766B and B.1 and the audiotape will be taken after we have had an opportunity to review the documents just now tendered. There is still a document pending that is D1818 and the same number .1, a translation introduced through Witness DP2. It's a statement given to the national authorities by a person who is not the witness. The admission of this document is rejected on the basis of lack of relevance. We then have document P2754, a UNMO daily SITREP relating to sniping from the house for the blind, introduced through Witness DP17, which was already introduced although not formally tendered through Witness van Baal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I don't know who DP17, the witness is at the moment, but I can't remember what this document is. I'd just like to check it. P2754?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would need more time, Ms. Pilipovic, then take your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there is no translation attached to it, Ms. Pilipovic, if you would like to consider it further.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I assumed. That's why I wanted to check this. And I will say what my position is on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the same would, I take it, be true for Prosecution Exhibit 2759, which is similar, also introduced through Witness DP17. Then the next exhibit would be D185A, introduced through the Witness Vorobev. It was a map provided by the Defence after the completion of the testimony upon the request of the Chamber. Madam Registrar, what is it? Number D185A? Yes. Then it's -- since it's requested by the Chamber, it's admitted into evidence. The next would be P3785, report of the Secretary-General on the fall of Srebrenica, introduced through Witness [redacted]. Ms. Pilipovic, I do not hear any objection; therefore, it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it was just one page from that document, but I can't remember right now, and I think that document was in English too, but I'm not sure, 3785. Perhaps my learned colleague will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was indeed -- excuse me. It was indeed in English, and my recollection is that there was more than one page that was relevant in order to place in context -- yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we started concentrating on one page but that we ended with the total document. It's not one page, as far as I can see. It is -- yes, we, I think, finally what was tendered was the document with the UN number A54549, report of the Secretary-General pursuant to General Assembly resolution 53/35, the fall of Srebrenica. It's my recollection that the context should be clear. Pages 31 and 32 of that document, which is paragraph D, deals with Markale massacre and disagreements on the use of air power, and it's there where some results of UNPROFOR investigations are presented. And one of the issues also was the footnotes that were contained in those pages, and therefore the pages 108 and 109, these are the pages with the footnotes, are part of the document as it has been tendered. So we finally now have five pages covering the whole paragraph on the Markale massacre and disagreements on the use of air power, page 31-32, and footnote pages 108 and 109.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to have a look at that document if I may and in fact you of the Defence's position on Friday, because I think that there was another report of that kind. I'm not sure. I'm not sure what resolution that report related to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you an opportunity to express yourself since it's only an English text, P3785. Then we have one document which has not been formally admitted into evidence, although it's a Chamber exhibit; that's C1. That's the original of Prosecution Exhibit 2506B, which is a medical certificate. The Chamber has requested this document, and it is now formally admitted under C1. Then, Madam Registrar, it becomes so complicated that I would like to ask you to guide us through a number of documents, and that is, I would say, the videotapes. That's P3793A, or am I now making a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now come to what I would like to call the Gray exhibits. We -- I think the major issue was the videotapes, rather than anything else. And if I am well informed, it was D348/20, to which the Prosecution wanted first to enquire into the source. I think that's the matter of the fifth tape as a potential source of one of the sequences on that videotape. Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Your Honour, the Defence has realised that there was a fifth tape. We only found that later. I think that the problem of that tape arose because initially there were four videotapes. Mr. Gray came to see me in my office. It's a small office, and he worked with my colleague on occasion. As far as I can remember, one tape had no purpose whatsoever, and I think that that is where the problem arose. I know that there were BBC tapes which have been disclosed. I don't know whether there were four BBC tapes; I can't say that at the moment. But as far as I have understood this, we believe that these tapes were of value. And I think that there was some confusion because it was a problem to provide cassettes that could be of use to our colleagues and to the Defence, cassettes that were of value, of importance. I think that this concerns a cassette on which you could see football matches for the entire duration of the tape. So in fact there were always four cassettes. I think that's the situation. As I have said, I didn't discuss the matter in detail with Mr. Gray, but I know that there were four tapes that were of importance, four quality tapes, and there was one that was useless so to say, and I think that's where the problem arose. Perhaps some cassettes got mixed up, but the essence of the matter is the -- the substance of the matter is that four cassettes were important. I don't think there was anything on the tape -- on one of the tapes that would have anything to do with the area that we are interested in. I didn't review -- I didn't view all the tapes entirely, but I did receive some copies from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would not mind that I stop you, Ms. Pilipovic. I think the issue is whether the compilation tape produced by the Defence would find any objections from the Prosecution and the Prosecution had difficulties in expressing itself because it didn't know where the first sequence came from. Meanwhile, I take it that the tape you're talking about has been disclosed to the Prosecution? That's a different issue, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the fifth tape has been disclosed to the Prosecution, Mr. President, and I don't object to the tender of the Defence compilation tape. You may recall, Mr. President, that when the first two clips, if I could call them that, or first clip of that tape was played, I immediately inquired through you of the Defence whether that indeed was on one of the four tapes they had disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I was assured that it was. I was repeatedly assured that it was. I was repeatedly informed that we had received all of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear that one of the parties, as I said at that time, caused a bad weekend for one of the other parties and it was still unknown at that very moment which one caused the bad weekend for the other one. I think this is what you're referring to at this moment, also looking at the clock, the most important for the Chamber to know is whether viewing the fifth tape would have any consequences for the admission of the tape initially tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It was on the fifth tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But I don't object to it. But there is another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the first has been settled. This fifth tape does not cause any objection to the admission of the compilation. But the other issue, is Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the other issue is this: The fifth tape comprised, I think, altogether some 12 BBC clips. Had that been disclosed to the Prosecution, it would have been the subject of cross-examination of Mr. Gray. There is no remedy to that situation we now find ourselves in. Having denied the existence of the fifth tape, we received it well after the witness had returned to New Zealand. Mr. President, I have arranged for three of those clips to be placed on a -- a blank tape, and I have a transcript of those clips. I seek to tender it. The relevance is that it goes to establishing a pre-indictment campaign of sniping and shelling and the infliction of terror on Sarajevan civilians. Mr. President, perhaps at this stage I could hand up a copy of the transcript which will give you some idea of the contents and provide a copy to my learned colleague to perhaps be translated to her by her assistant at some stage so that we could consider this further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to point out that the cassette number 5, as my colleague says, but I think that it's part of cassette 4, I'd like to say that I don't have a copy of that tape in order to be able to view all of this. I provided my colleagues with the original of the cassette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a copy made, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There isn't a full copy of the video. Perhaps that could be passed to Madam Registrar or perhaps it could be -- I have no objection to it being returned to the Defence on the understanding that once they've viewed it, until this issue is settled, it could then be passed to Madam Registrar, given the history of the matter. We still haven't received, Mr. President, a credible explanation as to why that was not provided when it should have been provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I suggest is that the original, for the time being, remains in the hands of the registry. This prevents any later debate on whether the excerpt made by the Prosecution would be -- would contain parts of that other tape. We could not check any more once it has been given back to one of the parties. There seems to be some difference of view in respect of the relevance of certain parts. I would, however -- I don't know how difficult this is with this tape. I would very much like to have a copy of that original tape, even not in evidence, to be kept by the -- perhaps marked for identification, kept by the registrar. I would like to give an opportunity to Ms. Pilipovic to see exactly what parts are tendered now. That means that you would now receive at least the tape containing the three parts that the Prosecution intends to tender so that you could at least see what that is and also look at the transcript of it so that the Defence is in a position to express itself next Friday on the issue. The original is where?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but I would also request a copy of the original cassette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Once -- we could ask to -- first of all, the original will be returned to you, and we could ask whether meanwhile a copy could be provided. But from these tapes, as you might remember, we are not always sure how much time it takes to copy them. That depends on the system used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it assists my learned colleague, perhaps I should indicate that I have not edited any of the three clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So they are completely whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So apart from that they are clips and therefore not the entirety of the tape, you didn't edit in whatever way the clips played. So Ms. Pilipovic, for the time being you have to do with the three clips selected by the Prosecution, and as soon as a copy of the original tape has been made, the original will be given back to you so that you can look at it. This is not to say that there will be another opportunity for you after this whole history to tender parts of it. But we'll see. You just to start with can look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the video is P3783 and the transcript is P3783A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then think that apart from that we still have to give a decision on this last video that is introduced not through a witness for the reasons set out by the Prosecution, that all the other Gray documents have meanwhile now been dealt with, because the others -- the total list were admitted on the 7th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we have to take a formal decision now on D348/20. That is the compilation tape tendered by the Defence with the different sequences on it. And an opportunity has been given to you, Ms. Pilipovic, to make whatever objection you would have with respect to the compilation video of the Prosecution, which was 3793A, because you had not seen it at that time. I think it was provisionally admitted into evidence. But an opportunity was given to you to make objections, once you had viewed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will inform you of my position on Friday. But could I have a copy of the videocassette by tomorrow in order to check whether it's from that-- whether it's from that cassette. In spite of -- given the fact I trust my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It had been given to you already. The compilation video was tendered. But at the moment where you had had no opportunity yet to review it. And therefore, since the Prosecution told us that these were just their selection of sequences, that it was admitted into evidence because they were played in court, those sequences, but you would have an opportunity to look at it and make any objections if you would deem necessary to do so. So one opportunity has been given. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understood that. But I just said that I wanted a copy of the original cassette that my colleagues used to make this transcript and these compilations. That's how I understood this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the originals were your originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar draws my attention to the possibility that you are confusing the compilation tape that has been given to you today, which is a compilation of three sequences that the Prosecution found on the tape that could not be found before, and the compilation tape provided earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that they disclosed and the one that we have viewed here. Yes, I have understood it now. There are two cassettes. The first one that was shown when Mr. Gray was heard and the copy I have been given now has to do with the cassette that was provided to my colleagues later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I will inform you of my position with regard to all the tapes on Friday, since my colleague dealt with this. I remember viewing these tapes, and I will express my position then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last issue we still have is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we had the issue of the Dunjic documents where the Defence would consider which would be tendered, and I do understand that all these documents are tendered, Ms. Pilipovic. These are mainly sketches, I would say, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I suggested to your associate to have all those sketches marked with one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll make it one set then. But then we should at least -- Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Madam Registrar just showed me the bundle. I would also call to the attention of the Chamber that included within that bundle are some excerpts from a book in B/C/S. And again, we have the situation where we do not have English translations of a number of pages, I would think four or five pages that are included in that bundle, and we would simply ask for the Defence position with respect to what the Chamber should do with those documents for which there's no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd also like to get a copy of this whole set of documents. As for the rest, we shall have the translations by Friday and we shall give them to our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll wait with the final decision until we have received the translation of those pages of a book. Then perhaps we should not start with that. We have one document which is the -- is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a document that has been shown to several witnesses, a document which initially was incomplete, page 2 missing. It is the report of the meeting with the presidents of the municipalities containing strategic goals, and a lot of attention has been paid to the fifth objective. We had an incomplete version. We had a translation related to the incomplete version but attached to the complete version we had one with one stamp, we had one with two stamps. We'll finally give a decision on that on Friday as well. And we'd like to -- if the parties could just very briefly put down on paper their position in respect to that document in all the versions we've seen until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did as ordered by the Chamber, and we made a submission stating the Defence's position with regard to the documents, how to put it, both the first and the second. I can only check the date on which we filed -- on which we filed it, but if need be we shall write it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do -- no, no, no. I do remember. You have argued that the second copy would show that the authenticity of the document is doubtful and that for that reason that it should not be admitted into evidence. We -- if there's any submission to be made by the Prosecution in respect of that document - but I think there was a response already - but we'll deal with the matter next Friday because it's now five minutes past 7.00. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not yet formally tendered the documents that went -- that were shown to the witness Richard Gray. The -- I don't know how you want to handle that, whether we do that or work on the basis that what documents he was shown are tendered. If it's the latter, Mr. President, there was a personal letter that was shown to him with a number of annexes. I would simply say in relation to that document that only those parts upon which he was examined or cross-examined should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be what number, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could indicate that on Friday, Mr. President. We don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with that on Friday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of Madam Registrar we could make a short list of those issues that are still outstanding so that we can deal with it on Friday and that we don't forget anything. We will then adjourn until next Friday at quarter past 2.00. And just to clarify the situation, at this moment apart from a few decisions that had to be taken, the Defence case has been closed, apart from those issues. We explained to the parties how we would proceed, that what we -- that was after one week -- one week after the closure of the Defence case. But of course we took a bit more time on the last expert witnesses, and we'll therefore try to continue with rebuttal evidence, if any, next Monday, as I explained before. We'll adjourn until next Friday, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of March, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
